property_summary: For any caller and any msg.value, the reference contract C accepts (does not revert) the fallback call exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant that requires 5 ether will accept different msg.value and thus the acceptance predicate differs (there exist inputs where C accepts but mutant reverts, and vice versa).

For any caller/address and any block timestamp, the reference contract's fallback accepts (does not revert) a call iff msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant instead accepts when msg.value == 5 ether, so there exist fuzzed msg.value inputs for which the reference accepts but the mutant reverts (and vice versa).

For every call to C's fallback, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) the call iff msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant instead accepts when msg.value == 5 ether, so there exist fuzzed msg.value inputs where the reference accepts but the mutant (requiring 5 ether) would reject and vice versa.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether, the reference contract only updates pastBlockTime when the block timestamp strictly increases (i.e. block.timestamp > pastBlockTime); the mutant removes that guard and therefore can update pastBlockTime even when timestamps do not increase.

For any call that sends exactly 10 ether to C, the reference contract only updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp strictly increases (so repeated identical-timestamp payments do not change pastBlockTime), whereas the mutant updates pastBlockTime even when timestamp does not increase, breaking the invariant that pastBlockTime remains unchanged if timestamp is unchanged.

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether, the reference contract never updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp is unchanged (i.e., pastBlockTime only increases when timestamp strictly increases); the mutant (which removes the timestamp check) can update pastBlockTime even when timestamp is unchanged, violating this invariant.

Invariant: after any fallback call that sends 10 ether, C.pastBlockTime is never set to a value less than or equal to its previous value unless the block.timestamp strictly increases; the mutant can overwrite pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp is equal to the prior pastBlockTime (i.e., it allows pastBlockTime to change without a strictly greater timestamp).

For any caller and any block timestamp, C only updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp is strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime; the mutant removes that guard and can change pastBlockTime even when timestamp does not advance, violating that invariant.

After any successful payable fallback call that requires msg.value == 10 ether and a strictly increasing wall-clock timestamp, the public getter pastBlockTime of the correct contract C is set to the current block.timestamp (so it is greater than its prior value); the mutant that writes block.number instead breaks this because pastBlockTime will instead equal the block number and thus may not be > previous pastBlockTime for some inputs.

After any successful payable fallback call providing exactly 10 ether and with block.timestamp strictly greater than the previous stored pastBlockTime, the contract's public getter pastBlockTime increases to equal the current block.timestamp; the mutant that assigns block.number instead can leave pastBlockTime not equal to the current block.timestamp for some inputs and thus violates this rule.

For every valid fallback invocation that increases block.timestamp, the reference contract never leaves any balance in C immediately after the call unless block.number % 15 != 0 (i.e. reference only drains balance when block.number % 15 == 0), whereas the mutant always drains balance on every such call — so the invariant is: if block.number % 15 != 0 then address(c).balance remains unchanged (not drained) after the call; the mutant violates this for some inputs.

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly increasing block.timestamp, the reference contract only pays out its full balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance == 0 after the call iff block.number % 15 == 0); the mutant inverts the condition and will pay out when block.number % 15 != 0, violating this rule for some block numbers.
